- If sentiment shows strong negative spikes (e.g., -1.00) in recent days, reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum to avoid overcorrection.  
- If model shows steep upward trend after a recent high, check for overshoot — cap forecast at 1–2% below recent peak if sentiment is neutral or negative.  
- If true outcome shows sharp downward correction after a forecast peak, model may be overestimating mean reversion — adjust downward by 5–10% of forecasted range.  
- When sentiment is consistently positive (e.g., 1.00) but true price drops, model may be overconfident — reduce forecast slope by 10–15% in next 5–7 days.  
- If forecast is rising steadily but true price shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of decline), reduce forecast slope by 5–10% and shift mean to lower end of range.  
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed, avoid aggressive trend extrapolation — use 3–5 day moving average of recent history as baseline for correction.  
- If forecast is consistently above true price by 5–10% over 3–5 days, reduce forecast by 5–10% and apply sentiment-weighted decay (e.g., -0.5x if sentiment = 0.00).  
- If sentiment shows strong positive momentum (e.g., 1.00) but price drops sharply, model may be overestimating bullish sentiment — reduce forecast by 5–10% and add 1–2 day lag correction.
